stem: A client awaiting surgery says, ‘I am terrified something will happen when I am under anesthesia.’ Which response by the nurse is best?

options.A: There is nothing to worry about because anesthesia is safe, so try not to think about it
options.B: Tell me what concerns you most about the anesthesia so we can address the questions and support you before the procedure
options.C: It is better not to discuss anesthesia now because talking about risks will usually make anxiety worse
options.D: Everyone feels the same before surgery, so your anxiety does not require individual assessment

rationale: Therapeutic communication begins by inviting the client to describe the specific concern and by listening without minimizing or making guarantees. The nurse can then reinforce appropriate preoperative information, use calming/supportive strategies, and ensure questions requiring detailed anesthesia risk-benefit discussion are addressed by the anesthesia provider.
educational_objective: Use open-ended, individualized therapeutic communication to assess preoperative anxiety before providing support or facilitating further education.
source_organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf
source_locator: Preoperative Nursing Care — Provide Emotional Support: address fears, anxiety and concerns through active listening, empathy and therapeutic communication; nurse reinforces information and addresses questions/concerns
source_claim_supported: Preoperative nurses assess and address anxiety using active listening, empathy, therapeutic communication and appropriate education/support.

correction_summary: Rebuilt the generic intervention list into an open-ended therapeutic-response item. Removed false reassurance, assumptions that all clients experience identical anxiety, and any implication that the nurse independently provides the anesthesia informed-consent discussion.
